collection.title: Entrepreneurship: Starting and Running a Small Business

questions.section_skill: Describe a business as solving a problem for paying customers
questions.outcome_title: Describe a business as solving a problem for customers who pay, and tell revenue-seeking activity from a hobby
questions.intro: A business sells something people want: a service, a product, a digital file, or content. An entrepreneur is a person who starts and runs a business and takes on its risk. The key test is simple: does it solve a problem or meet a want for customers who are willing to pay? A hobby is done mainly for enjoyment; it may sell sometimes, but it is not organized to earn money. A business plans to earn more than it spends over time, even if it starts small.
questions.prompt: Dana bakes bread for fun and gives it to friends. Which change would turn this into a business?

choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
She posts photos of her bread online each day.
She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.

questions.correct_answer: She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.
questions.feedback: A business needs customers who pay. Selling loaves to neighbors who pay is the change that matters.

wrong_choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: buying equipment alone does not create customers

wrong_choices.text: She posts photos of her bread online each day.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: posting photos does not involve customers paying

wrong_choices.text: She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: giving more away is still not selling to customers

questions.intro: Think of a lemonade stand. It has something to sell (lemonade), people who want it (thirsty walkers), and a price they pay. That is the core of any business: something people want, customers, and payment. If you take away the paying customers, you have a hobby or a gift. questions.section_skill: Compare a side business and a full-time business
questions.outcome_title: Compare a side business with a full-time business by time, income needs and risk
questions.intro: A side business runs alongside a job or school. A full-time business is your main work and main income. A side business usually has less risk, because a paycheck or other income still covers living costs while you test the idea, but it has less time. A full-time business has more time but more risk: if sales are slow, personal bills may go unpaid. Many owners start on the side, then decide later using evidence such as steady sales, savings and a clear plan.
questions.prompt: Mia works 40 hours a week and wants to test a pet-sitting idea. Which plan has the lower personal risk?

choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
Sign a long lease for a pet store
Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
Quit her job today to pet-sit full time

questions.correct_answer: Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
questions.feedback: Keeping her job while testing keeps her bills covered, so the personal risk is lower.

wrong_choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a large loan adds risk before demand is known

wrong_choices.text: Sign a long lease for a pet store
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a lease is a big commitment before testing

wrong_choices.text: Quit her job today to pet-sit full time
wrong_choices.why_wrong: this removes her steady income before the idea is tested

questions.intro: Documented history: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield took a $5 correspondence (mail) course in ice cream making from Penn State. In 1978 they opened their first scoop shop in a renovated gas station in Burlington, Vermont. They had first thought about bagels, but the equipment cost too much. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation, not their words): learn the skill cheaply, pick an idea whose start-up costs you can afford, and begin with one small location. One success story does not guarantee the same result for another business.

questions.section_skill: Identify a real, frequent customer problem
questions.outcome_title: Identify a specific, frequent problem that someone already spends time or money on
questions.intro: A good business idea starts with a real problem. A real problem happens often, matters to the person, and is something they already spend time or money trying to solve. "People might like this" is weak. "Parents in my neighborhood drive 30 minutes twice a week to a tutor" is strong, because it describes a costly habit that already exists. Look for complaints, workarounds (homemade fixes), and money already being spent.
questions.prompt: Which statement describes the strongest customer problem?

choices.text: Some people might enjoy a new kind of phone case someday.
Restaurant owners spend hours each week fixing their online menus.
My friends said a glow-in-the-dark mug sounds kind of fun.
Everyone would probably like more free time in their lives, so it is a problem.

questions.correct_answer: Restaurant owners spend hours each week fixing their online menus.
questions.feedback: Hours spent every week on a task is a frequent, costly problem people already deal with.

wrong_choices.text: Some people might enjoy a new kind of phone case someday.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: it is a guess with no sign of a costly habit

wrong_choices.text: My friends said a glow-in-the-dark mug sounds kind of fun.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a fun idea is not a problem people pay to fix

wrong_choices.text: Everyone would probably like more free time in their lives, so it is a problem.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: it is vague and names no specific habit

questions.section_skill: Write and judge a clear offer
questions.outcome_title: Write an offer (value proposition) that says who it is for, the problem and the result
questions.intro: An offer (also called a value proposition) says, in plain words, who it is for, what problem it solves, and what result the customer gets. A simple pattern: "For [customer] who [problem], we [what you do] so you can [result]." For example: "For busy pet owners who work late, we walk your dog at lunch so it gets exercise and you do not rush home." A clear offer is specific, honest and easy to repeat. It avoids vague phrases like "best quality" that do not say what the customer gets.

questions.feedback: It names the customer, the help and the result.

wrong_choices.text: Our company has many years of fitness experience in sports.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: it talks about the company, not the customer

wrong_choices.text: We offer the very best fitness services and the highest quality for all of you.

questions.intro: Documented history: Sara Blakely cut the feet off control-top pantyhose to wear under white pants. She started Spanx in 2000 with $5,000 of her own savings. Several hosiery manufacturers turned her down before one agreed to make the product, and she got it into the Neiman Marcus department store. Lesson drawn by this course (an interpretation, not her words): a problem you have yourself can be a starting point, but you still need evidence that many others share it and will buy. One success story does not guarantee the same result.

questions.intro: A customer interview is a short conversation to learn about someone's real problems. The most useful questions ask about what people already DID, not what they say they WOULD do. "Tell me about the last time you looked for a babysitter" gives real facts: how long it took, what they paid, what went wrong. "Would you use my babysitting app?" invites polite guesses. Past behavior is better evidence than predictions, because people are often too kind or too hopeful about the future.

wrong_choices.why_wrong: it asks for an opinion, not experience

questions.section_skill: Recognize and rewrite leading questions
questions.outcome_title: Recognize and rewrite leading or yes-pushing interview questions
questions.intro: A leading question pushes a person toward a particular answer. "Don't you hate waiting for the bus?" pushes toward yes. "Wouldn't it be great to have an app for that?" pushes toward praise. A neutral question lets the person answer honestly: "How do you usually get to work?" or "What, if anything, bothers you about your commute?" Leading questions make an idea look better than it is. Neutral questions, about real experience, make the results trustworthy.

Where do you usually buy desserts for family events?
What kind of cookies did you buy last time you shopped?

questions.feedback: It pushes the person toward agreeing.

wrong_choices.text: How often do you eat homemade baked goods each month?
Where do you usually buy desserts for family events?
What kind of cookies did you buy last time you shopped?

questions.section_skill: A push versus an open door
questions.outcome_title: Recognize and rewrite leading or yes-pushing interview questions
questions.intro: Picture two ways to ask about a restaurant. "The food was amazing, wasn't it?" is a push: the polite answer is yes. "How was the food?" is an open door: the person can say anything. Leading questions often include the answer you hope for, or words like "right?", "don't you", or "wouldn't it". An open door question asks "what", "how", or "when" and lets the person choose their own words.

A math question
An open door (neutral)
A yes-or-no fact check

questions.feedback: It suggests the hoped-for answer.

wrong_choices.text: A math question

questions.section_skill: Rank evidence of demand
questions.outcome_title: Rank evidence of demand, with payments and pre-orders above opinions
questions.intro: The strongest evidence that people want something is that they pay for it, or commit money in advance. From strongest to weakest: real purchases; paid pre-orders or deposits; signed agreements; sign-ups that ask for real effort, such as booking a time; email sign-ups; and finally compliments, likes and "I would buy that." Each step down costs the person less, so it means less. When testing an idea, aim for evidence near the top: something people give up money or real effort to get.

A hundred people visited the website once.
Twenty people said "I would buy that" at a party.

questions.correct_answer: Ten customers paid a deposit to reserve a spot.
questions.feedback: Paying a deposit means giving up money, the strongest signal.

wrong_choices.text: Fifty people liked a photo of the product online.
A hundred people visited the website once.
Twenty people said "I would buy that" at a party.
